paragraphs: Many sampling algorithms explore a probability distribution by simulating continuous dynamics. Using gradients computed from only part of the data can make these methods more scalable, but it introduces additional noise. Accounting for that noise has often required specialized arguments, making more elaborate stochastic-gradient samplers difficult to design and justify.

The paper introduces a general construction in which two matrices specify a continuous Markov process for sampling. Its completeness result says that any continuous Markov process that samples the target distribution can be expressed within this framework. This gives existing continuous-dynamics methods a shared mathematical description and reduces the need for separate sampler-specific proofs.

The authors also use the construction to develop stochastic gradient Riemann Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a new sampler whose dynamics adapt to the current state. Experiments with simulated data and streaming Wikipedia analysis indicate that it combines benefits of Riemann Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with stochastic-gradient scalability. The contribution therefore includes both a unifying construction and a concrete demonstration of how it supports new sampler designs.
neurips-2015-a-complete-recipe-for-stoch.tldr: A complete two-matrix framework unifies continuous-time sampling methods and supports the design of scalable stochastic-gradient samplers.

paragraphs: Linear value-function approximation represents the value of states through a weighted combination of basis functions. The choice of these functions determines what the approximation can express. This paper studies how to construct and refine them in Markov decision processes, placing several existing approaches within a common theoretical framework.

The framework includes Krylov bases and methods driven by Bellman error as special cases. It also provides a general procedure for refinements that account for the environment's dynamics. The authors derive approximation-error bounds for any algorithm that follows this framework, so the analysis applies to a family of construction methods rather than only one particular refinement rule.

A further connection uses ideas related to bisimulation metrics to interpret refinement as selecting representative prototypes. These prototypes must be sufficiently diverse to represent the given decision process. This perspective connects the algebraic task of expanding a basis with the more concrete task of choosing useful representatives, while keeping the dynamics central to how representation quality is assessed.
neurips-2015-basis-refinement-strategies.tldr: A unified framework explains how to refine value-function bases around an environment's dynamics and bounds the resulting approximation error.

paragraphs: Color constancy aims to recover surface colors despite the color cast introduced by illumination. This paper estimates that illumination using individual pixels' color and brightness statistics, without spatial arrangement or semantic context. Its central observation is that a pixel's brightness can provide useful evidence about its underlying chromaticity.

A classifier scores possible true chromaticities given luminance. For each observed pixel, candidate illuminants imply different possible underlying colors; the classifier turns these possibilities into evidence about the illuminant. Combining that evidence across pixels produces a scene-wide estimate. An initial classifier uses training-image histograms, which favor hues associated with smooth reflectance functions and neutral colors among brighter pixels.

The authors report that even this histogram-based method outperforms the color-constancy methods they compare against. They then learn the classifier end to end, adjusting its likelihoods through stochastic gradient descent to reduce final illumination-estimation errors. This improves accuracy further, especially in the high-error tail, suggesting that training for the final scene-level decision helps address the method's more difficult cases.
neurips-2015-color-constancy-by-learning.tldr: Learning how brightness relates to surface color enables accurate illumination estimation from pixel statistics alone.

paragraphs: Community detection seeks groups within a graph, and this paper approaches the task by changing how the graph is represented. Random walks produce an embedding in a space of measures: the objects being compared are distributions rather than ordinary coordinate vectors. A modified form of k-means then clusters this representation.

This separates the method into a random-walk representation stage and a clustering stage suited to that representation. The authors describe the resulting algorithm as fast and readily parallelizable. On standard random-graph benchmarks, including some with overlapping communities, they report performance that matches or exceeds previously known algorithms. Those comparisons provide empirical support across the benchmark settings considered.

The paper also establishes a linear-in-edges time guarantee for a particular stochastic block model. That guarantee requires both a lower bound on p and a sufficiently large gap between p and q, with thresholds depending on graph size. Thus, the theoretical result identifies conditions supporting efficient operation, while the benchmark results supply a separate empirical assessment of community-detection performance.
neurips-2015-community-detection-via-mea.tldr: Random-walk distribution embeddings followed by modified k-means yield a parallelizable community detector with competitive benchmark results and a conditional linear-time guarantee.

paragraphs: Scene labeling needs both local visual evidence and information about the surrounding scene. This paper adapts a recurrent convolutional network, originally proposed for object recognition, to combine these sources of information within its convolutional layers. The architecture adds recurrent connections between neighboring units inside a layer.

Each unit receives a constant feed-forward input from the preceding layer together with recurrent input from nearby units. As these recurrent updates repeat, information can reach the unit from a progressively larger region. Local feature processing therefore becomes sensitive to broader context through the same computation, integrating feature extraction and contextual adjustment instead of assigning them to separate modules.

The authors also introduce a multiscale version to make further use of context. On the Stanford Background and Sift Flow benchmarks, they report better accuracy and efficiency than many leading comparison models. These results support recurrence within convolutional layers as a useful mechanism for scene labeling, with the reported gains covering both labeling quality and computational efficiency in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2015-convolutional-neural-networ.tldr: Recurrent connections within convolutional layers expand visual context and improve scene-labeling accuracy and efficiency on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Dueling bandit problems involve learning from comparisons between alternatives. A difficulty arises when no single alternative beats every other one: a Condorcet winner may not exist. This paper instead measures performance relative to a Copeland winner, providing a target that is guaranteed to exist in the setting studied.

The authors propose two algorithms for different problem sizes. Copeland Confidence Bound is designed for relatively few alternatives, while Scalable Copeland Bandits is better suited to large collections. Both aim to limit cumulative regret relative to the Copeland benchmark, allowing the learning objective to remain meaningful even when pairwise preferences lack an overall Condorcet winner.

The theoretical contribution improves the dependence of regret bounds on the number of alternatives. Previous results either achieved O(K log T) with restrictive assumptions or O(K² log T) without them. The paper reports O(K log T) bounds without those restrictive assumptions, where K counts alternatives and T counts rounds. This combines a more broadly applicable winner criterion with improved scaling in the stated regret guarantees.
neurips-2015-copeland-dueling-bandits-36.tldr: Two dueling-bandit algorithms target Copeland winners and achieve O(K log T) regret bounds without requiring a Condorcet winner.

paragraphs: Embed to Control addresses learning and controlling nonlinear dynamical systems directly from pixel images. Its central task is to learn a latent representation that supports both image generation and control. The method places this representation inside a deep generative model belonging to the variational-autoencoder family.

The key structural requirement concerns how the latent state changes over time: its dynamics must be locally linear. This makes local evolution in the learned space compatible with a simpler dynamical description while the overall task involves nonlinear systems and image observations. The model learns to generate image trajectories, so the representation concerns sequences and their evolution rather than only isolated images.

The authors derive the model directly from an optimal-control formulation in latent space, making control part of the model's construction. They report support for long-term image-sequence prediction and strong performance across several complex control problems. These findings position E2C as a way to connect visual representation learning with dynamical modeling and action selection through one structured latent space.
neurips-2015-embed-to-control-a-locally-.tldr: Embed to Control learns locally linear latent dynamics from raw images to support sequence prediction and nonlinear-system control.

paragraphs: This paper develops a particle-based implementation of loopy belief propagation for pairwise Markov random fields with continuous states. Its main concern is where to place particles so that they efficiently represent each node's local belief. Poorly matched proposal distributions can waste computation on particles that contribute little to that representation.

The method adapts proposals from an exponential family, repeatedly updating their parameters through expectation propagation. The resulting particle estimates are consistent for the loopy-belief-propagation marginals as the particle count increases. The target of this consistency statement matters: it concerns the marginals produced by loopy belief propagation, rather than a separate claim that those marginals always equal the model's exact marginals.

The authors report greater accuracy, lower computational cost, and better empirical robustness than an earlier particle belief-propagation algorithm. The main implementation has per-iteration cost quadratic in particle count. An accelerated version reduces this to subquadratic cost while preserving consistency for the same target marginals, and its empirical performance is nearly as good as that of the original procedure.
neurips-2015-expectation-particle-belief.tldr: Adaptive particle proposals improve continuous-state loopy belief propagation, with a faster variant retaining consistent estimates of its marginals.

paragraphs: Models of large neural populations often explain many recorded spike trains through a smaller collection of hidden signals evolving over time. These latent signals provide a compact, denoised account of population activity and its correlations. However, commonly used Poisson observation models restrict how variable spike counts can be, potentially biasing covariance estimates.

The generalized count linear dynamical system retains the latent-dynamics approach while replacing the Poisson restriction with a broader exponential family for counts. This family includes Poisson, Bernoulli, negative binomial, and other distributions. That flexibility allows the observation model to accommodate counts with either less or more dispersion than the Poisson model permits.

The authors extend variational-inference techniques to make learning this richer model tractable. Applied to primate motor-cortex recordings, it improves on leading comparison methods in representing the data's variance structure and predicting held-out observations. These results indicate that modeling count variability more flexibly can improve both the description of recorded population activity and predictive performance in the evaluated neural data.
neurips-2015-high-dimensional-neural-spi.tldr: A more flexible count observation model improves latent neural-dynamics modeling and held-out prediction on primate motor-cortex data.

paragraphs: Block-coordinate methods optimize groups of variables in succession. Existing analyses of cyclic block-coordinate gradient descent gave an O(1/r) rate after r passes through all blocks, but their dependence on the number of blocks was unfavorable. The bounds were at least a factor of K worse than corresponding gradient or proximal-gradient bounds.

This paper sharpens that comparison in specified problem classes. For a family of quadratic problems with nonsmooth terms, cyclic block-coordinate proximal gradient matches the block-count dependence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods up to a squared-logarithmic factor. For general convex problems, an improved coordinate-gradient bound can also match gradient descent in certain scenarios.

These are improvements in theoretical guarantees, showing that the previously large block-count penalty need not appear in the analyzed cases. The analysis also does not depend on the order of updates within each cycle. Consequently, it covers methods that randomly permute the blocks without replacement, extending the results beyond algorithms that reuse one fixed cyclic order.
neurips-2015-improved-iteration-complexi.tldr: Sharper bounds substantially reduce the theoretical block-count penalty for cyclic coordinate methods in specified convex optimization settings.

paragraphs: Planning among multiple agents must account for the fact that different participants can pursue their own interests. This paper provides what the authors describe as the first expectation-maximization formalization of self-interested multiagent planning. It works with interactive partially observable Markov decision processes over an infinite horizon and with finitely nested agent models.

The formulation differs from expectation-maximization approaches for ordinary partially observable planning and cooperative multiagent problems. Its computational approach uses the graphical structure specific to interactive models. This matters because the relationships represented in that structure offer information about how to organize the planning computation, rather than treating the formulation as an undifferentiated optimization problem.

The paper introduces a block-coordinate-descent approach for additional speed and explores forward filtering followed by backward sampling. This latter procedure combines exact filtering with sampling to exploit the problem's structure. Together, these contributions connect a formal inference-based account of individual planning with computational strategies aimed at making that account more manageable in the stated infinite-horizon, finitely nested setting.
neurips-2015-individual-planning-in-infi.tldr: An expectation-maximization formulation connects self-interested multiagent planning with structured inference and block-coordinate optimization.

paragraphs: Some crowdsourcing tasks ask each worker to approve a fixed number of good alternatives. A natural aggregation rule counts approvals and selects the alternative with the largest total. This paper asks whether that familiar rule also identifies the alternative most likely to be best, given the collected votes.

The authors frame votes as noisy evidence within a probabilistic model. This separates the format of the input from the criterion used to choose a winner: receiving approval sets does not by itself settle how those sets should be interpreted statistically. The relevant question becomes whether maximizing the approval count agrees with selecting the most likely best alternative under the model.

The paper's theoretical and empirical findings generally support approval voting, while also identifying situations in which it is suboptimal. The result therefore qualifies the apparent inevitability of simple counting without rejecting its usefulness. Its contribution is to make aggregation an explicit inference question and show that the answer can depend on the probabilistic setting behind the observed approvals.
neurips-2015-is-approval-voting-optimal-.tldr: A noisy-voting framework shows that counting approvals usually selects the most likely best option, but can be suboptimal in some settings.

paragraphs: The Gaussian Process Convolution Model builds a stationary signal by passing continuous-time white noise through a linear filter that is itself drawn from a Gaussian process. This makes the filter something to learn probabilistically. Conditional on the filter, the resulting signal is also a Gaussian process, with a flexibly specified covariance kernel.

The same construction has a frequency-domain interpretation in which a Gaussian process specifies the signal's power spectral density. The authors develop a variational free-energy method using inducing variables across domains to learn the filter efficiently and infer the driving noise. This connects learning temporal dependence with estimating how signal power is distributed across frequencies.

The inference procedure yields closed-form probabilistic estimates of the covariance kernel and noise-free signal for denoising and prediction. It also provides closed-form expressions for an approximate posterior over spectral density. Validation uses synthetic and real-world signals. The overall contribution is a shared probabilistic model for signal reconstruction, prediction, and spectrum estimation, with uncertainty represented in the learned quantities.
neurips-2015-learning-stationary-time-se.tldr: A Gaussian-process model of random filters learns flexible stationary signal structure for denoising, prediction, and probabilistic spectrum estimation.

paragraphs: Deep generative models learn layered representations and can use their generative structure to infer properties of inputs. This paper focuses on improving their ability to make accurate predictions. It introduces max-margin deep generative models, which incorporate a discriminative learning principle while preserving the model's capacity to generate data.

The approach brings max-margin learning into the generative-model framework so that predictive separation becomes an explicit training concern. To optimize the resulting piecewise-linear objective, the authors develop an efficient doubly stochastic subgradient algorithm. The contribution therefore includes both a combined modeling approach and an optimization procedure suited to its objective.

Experiments on MNIST and SVHN show that max-margin training can substantially improve prediction while retaining generative ability. When deep convolutional networks serve as both recognition and generative models, the resulting systems are competitive with leading fully discriminative networks. These findings support the possibility of strong classification within a generative framework, rather than requiring the model to give up its generative functionality to obtain the reported predictive gains.
neurips-2015-max-margin-deep-generative-.tldr: Max-margin training improves deep generative models' predictions while retaining generation, with competitive results on MNIST and SVHN.

paragraphs: Particle filtering approximates difficult probability distributions through a sequence of simpler sampling problems. Its accuracy depends heavily on the proposal distribution that generates candidate particles. This paper develops a way to adapt that proposal automatically, using an approximation to the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the posterior and proposal.

The framework accepts parameterized proposal families and supports both online and batch adaptation. Using neural networks for the proposals produces Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo. Richer learned proposals are intended to place particles where they better represent the posterior, linking adaptive particle methods with ideas from scalable variational inference.

Experiments show improved inference in a nonlinear state-space model compared with adaptive proposals including Extended Kalman and Unscented Particle Filters. Better inference also improves parameter learning when the method is used inside Particle Marginal Metropolis Hastings. Finally, it trains a latent-variable recurrent network with competitive music-modeling results. These findings demonstrate benefits both for posterior estimation itself and for learning procedures that depend on those estimates.
neurips-2015-neural-adaptive-sequential-.tldr: Neural networks adapt particle-filter proposals to improve inference and downstream learning in the evaluated sequential models.

paragraphs: The Newton–Stein method targets maximum-likelihood estimation in generalized linear models when observations greatly outnumber coefficients, while the coefficient count is itself substantial. In this regime, approximate curvature information can help optimization progress rapidly. The paper develops a way to obtain that information with a modest cost per iteration.

Its central move is to treat curvature construction as an estimation problem and apply a Stein-type lemma. This formulation also permits subsampling and eigenvalue thresholding to improve the procedure. The resulting algorithm aims to capture the fast progress associated with second-order methods while reducing the computational burden of obtaining the curvature information they use.

The convergence analysis assumes independently and identically distributed design-matrix rows with bounded support. Under the analyzed setting, convergence has a quadratic phase followed by a linear phase. Experiments on several datasets report the strongest performance among the algorithms compared. The theoretical and empirical contributions thus address complementary questions: how the iterations behave under stated assumptions and how the method performs in the evaluated optimization tasks.
neurips-2015-newton-stein-method-a-secon.tldr: Newton–Stein estimates curvature efficiently for generalized linear models, combining modest iteration costs with fast convergence under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Optimization Monte Carlo performs inference for simulator-based models without requiring a likelihood evaluation. It begins by making the simulator's random inputs explicit. Once a particular random-number vector is fixed, the simulated output becomes deterministic, allowing an optimization procedure to search for parameters whose simulated summaries resemble those of the observed data.

Repeating this process for different random-number vectors produces a collection of fitted parameter samples. The method then weights them using the prior and a Jacobian correction. That correction accounts for the change in volume between summary-statistic space and parameter space. The authors show that the weighted collection gives a Monte Carlo estimate of the posterior distribution.

Each sample's optimization can run independently, making the method readily parallelizable across computing nodes. It also supports an anytime strategy that directs additional resources toward the worst-performing sample. Validation uses six experiments. The contribution connects deterministic optimization under fixed simulator randomness with weighted probabilistic inference, while providing a computation structure that supports both parallel work and incremental refinement.
neurips-2015-optimization-monte-carlo-ef.tldr: Fixing simulator randomness turns likelihood-free inference into independent optimization problems whose weighted solutions estimate the posterior.

paragraphs: This paper revisits estimation in Latent Dirichlet Allocation through moment matching, an approach that learns model structure from statistical summaries of observations. The authors draw explicit connections between LDA and discrete forms of independent component analysis. Those connections supply both new statistical quantities to estimate and different computational tools for using them.

The first contribution is a new collection of tensors based on cumulants, with improved sample complexity. The second imports joint diagonalization techniques from independent component analysis to improve on approaches using the tensor power method. These address separate parts of estimation: which statistical summaries are constructed and how those summaries are processed to recover the model.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets evaluate the combination of the new tensors with orthogonal joint diagonalization. The authors report that this combination outperforms existing moment-matching methods. The significance is that a connection between two modeling traditions leads to practical changes in the estimation pipeline, supported by both a sample-complexity improvement and empirical comparisons of the resulting method.
neurips-2015-rethinking-lda-moment-match.tldr: Connections between LDA and discrete independent component analysis yield improved statistical tensors and more effective moment-matching estimation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an information-theoretic definition of visual saliency, seeking a shared account of what makes parts of visual data stand out. The definition connects with established work on scale space, interest-point detection, bilateral filtering, and previous saliency models. Its aim is therefore both explanatory and computational.

Using the proposed definition, the authors obtain results competitive with leading methods on two distinct tasks: predicting human eye fixations and segmenting salient objects. These tasks test different uses of saliency, one concerned with where people look and the other with identifying prominent objects. The reported results support the usefulness of the definition across both applications.

The paper also examines robustness to image transformations and extensions beyond images, using three-dimensional meshes as an example. More broadly, it relates saliency to visual information processing and discusses possible mechanisms in human vision. These connections provide a wider interpretation of the model, while the proposed links to human mechanisms remain suggestive rather than an established account of how biological vision computes saliency.
neurips-2015-saliency-scale-and-informat.tldr: An information-theoretic definition connects several saliency-related methods and delivers competitive fixation-prediction and salient-object segmentation results.

paragraphs: When a decision-making policy is updated repeatedly, its future behavior must be assessed under uncertainty. This paper studies that assessment for a class of iterative stochastic policy-optimization problems. It analyzes each newly updated policy, focusing on expected cost and the probability that the policy will violate constraints.

The approach uses empirical runs together with concentration inequalities to provide high-confidence performance assessments. A central difficulty is that policy adaptation changes the probability distribution governing outcomes. The authors derive a new inequality that accounts for the resulting change-of-measure likelihood ratio even when that ratio may be unbounded, addressing a complication created by the iterative learning process itself.

The resulting bound serves as a high-confidence certificate for future performance or safety. Such a certificate quantifies expected cost or violation probability rather than asserting that every future run is safe. The paper illustrates the approach with a simple robot-control scenario and presents preliminary steps toward aerial-vehicle navigation, distinguishing the demonstrated example from the more challenging applications being explored.
neurips-2015-sample-complexity-bounds-fo.tldr: A concentration bound accounts for iterative policy changes to certify future expected costs and constraint-violation probabilities with high confidence.

paragraphs: The paper considers parties that each hold a private bit and want to compute a function involving everyone's bits. Different parties may want different functions, and a central observer may have a separate objective. Privacy must leave uncertainty about an individual's bit even when the interaction transcript and every other bit are known.

The main result establishes the optimality of a simple noninteractive protocol in this setting. Each participant sufficiently randomizes their own bit and shares the privatized result. Despite allowing interactive computation in the problem formulation, the authors show that this direct sharing procedure attains optimal accuracy under the privacy requirements they study.

The result covers arbitrary functions and distortion measures, different privacy requirements for different participants, and both average and worst-case accuracy over inputs. Its breadth means that the optimality does not rely on all participants wanting the same computation or measuring error identically. The scope remains the stated private-bit setting, within which the theorem gives a strong justification for a particularly simple communication protocol.
neurips-2015-secure-multi-party-differen.tldr: For the studied private-bit computation setting, sharing independently privatized bits is optimal across broad function, privacy, and accuracy requirements.

paragraphs: Chain graphs under the interpretation studied here combine asymmetric relationships, as in Bayesian networks, with symmetric relationships, as in Markov random fields. When some variables are hidden, the distributions over the remaining variables can form a complicated model. This paper seeks a more manageable graphical description of those observable distributions.

The authors introduce mixed graphs called segregated graphs and associate them with models through a Markov property. These models are supermodels of chain-graph marginals: they contain the marginal distributions and are defined using conditional-independence restrictions. This makes the representation a structured enlargement of the marginal model rather than a claim to capture all of its possible constraints exactly.

Special properties of segregated graphs yield a natural factorization and allow many results from chain graphs and ordinary Markov models to carry over. The authors interpret this as evidence that segregated graphs provide an analogue of the ordinary Markov model for chain-graph marginals. The contribution supplies mathematical structure for reasoning about hidden variables in models that mix symmetric and asymmetric relationships.
neurips-2015-segregated-graphs-and-margi.tldr: Segregated graphs provide factorized conditional-independence supermodels for chain-graph distributions with hidden variables.

paragraphs: Stochastic variance-reduced gradient methods use a control variate to reduce the noise in gradient updates. This paper studies how to make those methods more economical in their gradient calculations. Its first result shows that the convergence rate can be preserved when errors in the control variate follow an appropriate decreasing sequence.

That result motivates variants with growing batches. Early iterations can use less expensive estimates, with larger batches introduced as optimization progresses and the required error decreases. The authors also show how support vectors can reduce gradient computations later in optimization. These strategies address different stages of training rather than assuming the same amount of gradient work is useful throughout.

Further analysis justifies a commonly used regularized SVRG update and shows that it improves the convergence rate. The paper also considers alternative ways to select minibatches and examines generalization error. Together, these contributions connect practical implementation choices with convergence analysis, identifying ways to reduce computation while retaining the stated rate guarantees under the required conditions on estimation error.
neurips-2015-stopwasting-my-gradients-pr.tldr: Practical SVRG variants reduce gradient work through controlled approximation, growing batches, and support-vector exploitation while preserving stated convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Spectral methods for learning dynamical systems can offer a useful balance of computational and statistical efficiency. However, adapting them to incorporate prior information, such as sparsity or other structure, can be awkward. This paper reformulates dynamical-system learning as a sequence of ordinary supervised-learning problems to make such adaptation easier.

The reformulation allows familiar supervised-learning tools to encode prior knowledge, including L1 regularization. Many existing spectral methods appear within the framework as cases that use linear regression. This gives them a shared interpretation while opening the supervised-learning component to alternatives that can express different assumptions about the desired representation.

The authors demonstrate examples in which nonlinear regression or lasso produces better state representations than plain linear regression. Their general analysis supplies correctness results for these instances. The contribution is therefore both a unification and an extension: it explains existing methods through standard prediction tasks and shows how changing those tasks' learners can improve representations in the examples studied, with theoretical support carried through the common framework.
neurips-2015-supervised-learning-for-dyn.tldr: Recasting dynamical-system learning as supervised learning makes sparsity and nonlinear predictors available within a unified, theoretically supported framework.

paragraphs: Asynchronous execution and reduced-precision arithmetic can accelerate stochastic gradient descent, but they also create noise that complicates convergence analysis. This paper develops a martingale-based framework designed to handle the richer noise patterns introduced by these implementation choices. The aim is to analyze efficient execution strategies within a shared mathematical approach.

The framework is applied in three ways. It gives convergence rates for convex Hogwild-style optimization under relaxed sparsity assumptions. It also analyzes asynchronous stochastic-gradient algorithms for nonconvex matrix problems, including matrix completion. Finally, it supports the design and analysis of Buckwild, an asynchronous algorithm that uses lower-precision arithmetic.

These applications connect theoretical analysis with choices that affect how training runs on hardware. The authors report experiments showing efficient execution across a variety of problems on modern hardware. The results support the practical value of the analyzed algorithms, while the theory provides convergence arguments for the particular convex, matrix, and reduced-precision settings addressed rather than a blanket guarantee for every asynchronous optimization problem.
neurips-2015-taming-the-wild-a-unified-a.tldr: A martingale-based analysis supports asynchronous and reduced-precision SGD, including relaxed Hogwild assumptions and the new Buckwild algorithm.
